nodes.label: Wanders et al. (1989) reported on sudden infant death in relation to long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase. Only the title was available, so no further detail can be given.

Rocchiccioli et al. (1990) described a child who presented in early childhood with episodes of coma and hypoglycemia and a rapidly progressive myopathy and cardiomyopathy, leading to death at 9 months of age. Ketosis was decreased (blood beta-hydroxybutyrate 0.07 mmol/L) even though plasma fatty acid levels were normal (0.81 mmol/L).

Rocchiccioli et al. (1990) found that the patient's urine contained excessive C6 to C10 dicarboxylic acids and, by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, an accumulation of medium- and long-chain (C8 to C14) 3-hydroxydicarboxylic acids, suggesting a defect of the mitochondrial enzyme that dehydrogenates 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA esters.

Rocchiccioli et al. (1990) showed impaired medium- and long-chain fatty acid oxidation in the patient's cultured fibroblasts and identified deficiency of long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase; activities of long-, medium-, and short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenases and 3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase were normal. They concluded that the disorder affects liver, skeletal muscle, and myocardium.

Rocchiccioli et al. (1990) noted that LCHAD deficiency shares many clinical similarities with systemic carnitine deficiency and with CPT and LCAD deficiencies, and that differential diagnosis relies on showing long-chain urinary 3-hydroxydicarboxylic acids and measuring enzyme activity in cultured fibroblasts.

Hagenfeldt et al. (1990) described 5 patients with a suspected defect in fatty acid beta-oxidation. During acute illness, they excreted massive amounts of 3-hydroxydicarboxylic acids in the urine and accumulated 3-hydroxy fatty acids in serum. Four of the patients died of cardiomyopathy and liver insufficiency between 3 and 14 months of age. Two of the patients had older sibs who had died unexpectedly in early infancy.

Hagenfeldt et al. (1990) found normal long-chain and medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase activities in fibroblasts from all 5 patients with 3-hydroxydicarboxylic aciduria. They concluded that these patients differed from previously described patients with beta-oxidation defects.

Jackson et al. (1991) described 2 children with long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency who both presented with an acute metabolic crisis and hypoglycemia, and who excreted even-chain unsubstituted dicarboxylic and 3-hydroxy-dicarboxylic acids in the urine.

Jackson et al. (1991) found low activity of long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase but normal activity of short-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase in cultured skin fibroblasts from 2 patients; the defect was further characterized by immunoprecipitating the short-chain enzyme using monospecific antibodies.

Jackson et al. (1991) suggested that LCHAD deficiency is probably inherited as an autosomal recessive trait, since intermediate enzyme activity was found in fibroblasts from the parents of one affected child.

Duran et al. (1991) reported 2 sibs with long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. One sib died suddenly and unexpectedly on the third day of life with extreme hypoketotic hypoglycemia. The younger sib, a girl, developed feeding problems, lowered consciousness, and liver dysfunction at age 5 months, and had signs of cardiomyopathy.

Duran et al. (1991) found large amounts of C6-C14 3-hydroxydicarboxylic acids and conjugated 3-hydroxyoctanoic acid in the urine of the surviving patient by GC/MS, and increased plasma long-chain acylcarnitine. A phenylpropionic acid loading test revealed small but significant amounts of conjugated 3-hydroxyphenylpropionic acid in urine, and LCHAD activity was deficient in cultured skin fibroblasts.

Duran et al. (1991) noted that a phenylpropionic acid loading test, which revealed urinary conjugated 3-hydroxyphenylpropionic acid (phenylhydracrylic acid), provided a clue to the diagnosis of LCHAD deficiency, subsequently confirmed by enzyme assay in fibroblasts.

Duran et al. (1991) prescribed a diet enriched in medium-chain triglycerides based on an MCT load; on this regimen the patient thrived, signs of cardiomyopathy disappeared, and liver function normalized.
Jackson et al. (1992) described a young girl who had recurrent episodes of muscle weakness that culminated in a severe attack of generalized muscle weakness.

In the patient described by Jackson et al. (1992), muscle mitochondria showed an abnormal pattern of beta-oxidation intermediates with accumulation of 3-hydroxyacyl- and 2-enoyl-CoA and carnitine esters and 3-oxoacylcarnitines. Long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase activity was low in mitochondria from all tissues, long-chain 2-enoyl-CoA hydratase activity was low in muscle mitochondria, and 3-oxoacyl-CoA thiolase activity with 3-oxohexadecanoyl-CoA was low in fibroblast, muscle, and cardiac mitochondria, with only partial deficiency when measured with 3-oxooctanoyl-CoA.

Jackson et al. (1992) found that long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase and long-chain 3-oxoacyl-CoA thiolase activities in fibroblasts from the patient's parents were intermediate between those of controls and the patient, and concluded that the combined defect appeared to be inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.

Jackson et al. (1992) concluded that the patient had a combined defect of long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase, long-chain 3-oxoacyl-CoA thiolase, and long-chain 2-enoyl-CoA hydratase, and suggested that a multifunctional enzyme catalyzes these activities in human mitochondria and is deficient in the patient.

Wanders et al. (1992) described a patient with clear signs of a mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation disorder. The patient's fibroblasts showed impaired palmitate beta-oxidation and a combined deficiency of long-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase, long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase, and long-chain 3-oxoacyl-CoA thiolase.

Using size-exclusion chromatography, Wanders et al. (1992) showed that this patient lacked the membrane-bound multifunctional beta-oxidation enzyme protein, which carries all 3 activities. They proposed that trifunctional protein deficiency is a new disorder of mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation, separate from isolated deficiency of a single enzyme activity.

Bertini et al. (1992) described an 11-month-old girl with acute episodes of hypoglycemia and hepatic encephalopathy reminiscent of Reye syndrome, along with 3-hydroxydicarboxylic aciduria. She had severe sensory-motor neuropathy, pigmentary retinopathy, and cardiomyopathy, and died of cardiac failure. Peripheral nerve pathology showed axonal neuropathy and demyelination. The authors noted that peripheral nerve involvement and retinal pigmentary degeneration had not been described before in patients with proven defects of mitochondrial beta-oxidation.
Bertini et al. (1992) found a deficiency of mitochondrial long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase in cultured fibroblasts from their patient.

Wilcken et al. (1993) reported 11 pregnancies in 5 mothers; 6 of the babies had LCHAD deficiency, and each of these pregnancies was complicated by features such as maternal fatty liver and HELLP (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) syndrome. By contrast, 3 of the mothers also gave birth to unaffected babies, and these pregnancies were largely uncomplicated.

Wilcken et al. (1993) concluded that a fetus with LCHAD deficiency may have adverse effects on maternal liver function, and that maternal heterozygosity alone cannot account for these effects because the complications segregated with fetal LCHAD status.

In patients with long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (LCHAD) deficiency, IJlst et al. (1994) sequenced the cDNAs encoding the alpha- and beta-subunits of the mitochondrial trifunctional protein and identified a G-to-C mutation at nucleotide 1528 (G1528C) in the 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase-encoding region of the alpha subunit, resulting in a glutamate/glutamine substitution at amino acid position 510. The change creates a PstI restriction site; by RFLP analysis, 24 of 26 unrelated patients expressed only the C1528 allele and the other 2 were heterozygous. The mutation was not found in 55 control subjects.

IJlst et al. (1994) found the G1528C mutation in the alpha subunit of mitochondrial trifunctional protein in all 26 unrelated LCHAD-deficient patients studied (only the mutant allele expressed in 24, heterozygous in 2) and in none of 55 controls, indicating a high frequency of this mutation among patients with LCHAD deficiency.

IJlst et al. (1994) noted that the mitochondrial trifunctional protein, involved in mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation, harbors long-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase, long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase, and long-chain 3-ketothiolase activities.

Sewell et al. (1994) reported a patient with long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency who presented with hypoketotic hypoglycemia, hepatopathy, secondary carnitine deficiency, and increased plasma long-chain acylcarnitines. The authors noted that the disorder, newly recognized, usually has a fatal outcome, and compared their patient with those in the literature.
Sewell et al. (1994) found 3-hydroxydicarboxylic aciduria in their patient, and the diagnosis of LCHAD deficiency was confirmed by studies in cultured skin fibroblasts.

Fryburg et al. (1994) described a black boy with features of Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba syndrome (BRRS) who also had a defect in long-chain fatty acid oxidation, expressed in cultured skin fibroblasts as LCHAD deficiency. He also had an abnormal brain MRI and enlargement of both lower limbs. The authors postulated that LCHAD deficiency may be the cause of the lipid myopathy in BRRS.

Fryburg et al. (1994) showed that cultured skin fibroblasts from a boy with Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba syndrome features had a defect in long-chain fatty acid oxidation, expressed as a deficiency of long-chain L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase activity.

Treem et al. (1994) reported a full-term infant who seemed normal at birth and presented at 4 months of age with hypoglycemia, coma and profound hepatic steatosis. The infant was found to have long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. The mother had had acute fatty liver of pregnancy during this pregnancy.

Treem et al. (1994) found that the mother of the LCHAD-deficient infant was heterozygous for the defect. They hypothesized that some cases of acute fatty liver of pregnancy are caused by the interaction between an affected fetus and a mother who is heterozygous for this fatty acid oxidation defect in the late third trimester.

Sims et al. (1995) studied 3 families with LCHAD deficiency in which the children had sudden unexplained death or hypoglycemia with abnormal liver enzymes (Reye-like syndrome). In all 3 families, the mothers had acute fatty liver of pregnancy with severe complications while pregnant with the affected infants.

Sims et al. (1995) used SSCV analysis of the exons of the LCHAD (trifunctional protein alpha subunit) gene and found 2 affected children homozygous for a G-to-C change at nucleotide 1528 (G1528C). The change lies in the LCHAD domain and replaces glutamic acid with glutamine at residue 474 of the mature alpha subunit (E474Q).

Sims et al. (1995) found that a third child with LCHAD deficiency was compound heterozygous for the G1528C (E474Q) mutation and a C1132T mutation. The C1132T change creates a premature stop codon at residue 342.

Sims et al. (1995) concluded that mutations in the LCHAD domain of the trifunctional protein alpha subunit in affected offspring are associated with maternal acute fatty liver of pregnancy. This was the first delineation of the molecular basis of isolated LCHAD deficiency.
Sims et al. (1995) noted that LCHAD catalyzes the third step of mitochondrial beta-oxidation. Its activity sits on the C-terminal portion of the alpha subunit of mitochondrial trifunctional protein.

IJlst et al. (1996) found the G1528C mutation in the cDNA for the alpha subunit of mitochondrial trifunctional protein at an allele frequency of 87% in 34 patients with LCHAD deficiency. When they expressed the wildtype and mutant proteins in S. cerevisiae, they showed that the G1528C mutation directly causes the loss of LCHAD activity.

IJlst et al. (1996) developed a method for detecting the G1528C mutation in genomic DNA. Because the mutation had an allele frequency of 87% among LCHAD-deficient patients, they suggested the test was valuable for prenatal diagnosis.
IJlst et al. (1996) showed that the gene encoding the alpha subunit of mitochondrial trifunctional protein is located on chromosome 2p24.1-p23.3.

IJlst et al. (1996) noted that in most patients only the LCHAD activity of mitochondrial trifunctional protein is deficient, while its long-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase and long-chain 3-ketothiolase activities are near normal. They described the deficiency as impairing oxidation of long-chain fatty acids, which can lead to sudden infant death.
IJlst et al. (1996) stated that this inborn error of fatty acid oxidation is very frequent, second only to medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency.

Tyni et al. (1997) reported the clinical findings in 13 patients with LCHAD deficiency. At presentation, during the first 2 years of life, the patients had hypoglycemia, cardiomyopathy, muscle hypotonia, and hepatomegaly. Seven patients had recurrent metabolic crises and 6 had a steadily progressive course. Two patients had cholestatic liver disease, which the authors noted is uncommon in beta-oxidation defects; 1 had peripheral neuropathy; and 6 had retinopathy with focal pigmentary aggregations or retinal hypopigmentation.

Tyni et al. (1997) found dicarboxylic aciduria in 9 of 10 patients with LCHAD deficiency tested, and most patients had lactic acidosis, increased serum creatine kinase activity, and low serum carnitine concentration. Enoyl-CoA hydratase and 3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase activities of the mitochondrial trifunctional protein were variably decreased in skin fibroblasts.
Tyni et al. (1997) found bilateral periventricular or focal cortical lesions on neuroimaging in 3 of 13 patients with LCHAD deficiency and brain atrophy in 1.
Tyni et al. (1997) reported that all 13 patients with LCHAD deficiency were homozygous for the common G1528C mutation.

Tyni et al. (1997) reported that only 1 of 13 patients with LCHAD deficiency, who had received dietary treatment for 9 years, was alive at 14 years of age; all of the others died before 2 years of age. The authors suggested that early dietary management may change the otherwise poor prognosis.

Schrijver-Wieling et al. (1997) reported 2 girls with LCHAD deficiency, aged 8 and 15 years. Both had extensive macular pigment deposits and a 'salt and pepper' scattering of pigment in the retina, and both had decreasing visual acuity.

Schrijver-Wieling et al. (1997) noted that LCHAD deficiency, a defect of fatty acid breakdown, is associated with life-threatening episodes of hypoketotic hypoglycemia during prolonged fasting. They also noted that neuropathy and retinal pigment changes had been mentioned in only a few cases.

Schrijver-Wieling et al. (1997) noted that patients tend to have no symptoms between attacks. They recommended that testing for LCHAD deficiency be included in the workup of children with retinal dystrophy, especially when other clinical symptoms have occurred. They said early recognition could increase life expectancy by avoiding catabolism and by using appropriate diets.
Uusimaa et al. (1997) reported 2 patients with L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency who had pigmentary retinopathy.

Ibdah et al. (1999) studied 24 children with 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. Nineteen had a deficiency only of long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase and presented with hypoketotic hypoglycemia and fatty liver.

Ibdah et al. (1999) used DNA amplification and nucleotide-sequence analysis of the alpha subunit of the mitochondrial trifunctional protein in children with isolated LCHAD deficiency. Eight children were homozygous for a glu474-to-gln (E474Q) mutation. Eleven others were compound heterozygous for this mutation and a different mutation on the other allele.

Ibdah et al. (1999) found that 79% of heterozygous mothers had acute fatty liver of pregnancy or HELLP syndrome while carrying fetuses with the Glu474Gln mutation. The authors concluded that women with acute liver disease during pregnancy may have the Glu474Gln mutation, and that their infants are at risk for hypoketotic hypoglycemia and fatty liver.

Ibdah et al. (1999) described 5 other children with complete trifunctional protein deficiency, meaning loss of activity of all 3 enzymes. These children presented with neonatal dilated cardiomyopathy or progressive neuromyopathy. None had the Glu474Gln mutation, and none of their mothers had liver disease during pregnancy.

Ibdah et al. (1999) described an infant with LCHAD deficiency that had not been suspected. At 2 months of age the infant presented with acute infantile hypocalcemia and vitamin D deficiency, together with occult, unexplained cholestatic liver disease. The infant died suddenly and unexpectedly at 8 months. The authors concluded that infantile hypocalcemia is an unusual phenotype associated with LCHAD deficiency.

In the infant with LCHAD deficiency who presented with hypocalcemia and cholestasis, Ibdah et al. (1999) found by molecular analysis that the infant was homozygous for the common LCHAD mutation 1528G-C (E474Q).

Ibdah et al. (1999) reported that the mother of the LCHAD-deficient infant had preeclampsia in the third trimester of that pregnancy. In a later pregnancy she developed severe acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP), and the fetus died in utero at 33 weeks' gestation. The authors concluded that fetal LCHAD deficiency is associated with a range of maternal illnesses, from preeclampsia to life-threatening AFLP.
Thiel et al. (1999) reported long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (LCHAD) deficiency that showed itself in the newborn period on the first day of life, presenting with tachypnea.

Carpenter and Wilcken (1999) reported a neonatal diagnosis of long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (LCHAD) deficiency and discussed what it means for newborn screening by tandem mass spectrometry.

Van Hove et al. (2000) reviewed the acylcarnitines in plasma and blood spots of 23 patients with proven LCHAD deficiency. The long-chain 3-hydroxyacylcarnitines C14:1, C14, C16 and C18:1 were elevated, as were the long-chain acylcarnitines C12, C14:1, C14, C16, C18:2 and C18:1. Acetylcarnitine was decreased.

Van Hove et al. (2000) found that, in plasma, hydroxy-C18:1 acylcarnitine above the 95th centile of controls, combined with elevation of two of the three acylcarnitines C14, C14:1 and hydroxy-C16, identified over 85% of LCHAD-deficient patients with a false-positive rate below 0.1%. Diagnostic specificity was lower in blood spots than in plasma because normal erythrocytes contain high endogenous levels of long-chain acylcarnitines. The profile was also diagnostic in asymptomatic patients and was not influenced by genotype.

Van Hove et al. (2000) found that a diet low in fat and high in medium-chain triglyceride lowered all disease-specific acylcarnitines in LCHAD-deficient patients, often to normal levels. They suggested that the assay is useful for monitoring treatment.

Ibdah et al. (2001) performed molecular prenatal diagnosis in 9 pregnancies: 8 in 6 families with isolated LCHAD deficiency and 1 in a family with complete mitochondrial trifunctional protein (TFP) deficiency, using chorionic villus samples in 7 and amniocytes in 2. The fetal genotype was identified in all 9 pregnancies; 2 fetuses were affected (pregnancies terminated), 2 had a normal genotype, and 5 were heterozygotes. Genotypes were confirmed by molecular analysis and enzymatic assays in the aborted fetuses and neonates, and the authors concluded that molecular prenatal diagnosis is possible and valid in families with known TFP defects.

Ibdah et al. (2001) found that the 7 pregnancies in which women heterozygous for TFP alpha-subunit mutations carried fetuses with wild-type or heterozygous genotypes were uncomplicated, and all offspring were alive and apparently healthy.

den Boer et al. (2002) reviewed questionnaire data on 50 of 61 unselected patients with LCHAD deficiency diagnosed at their center. The mean age at clinical presentation was 5.8 months (range, 1 day to 26 months), and 7 (15%) presented in the neonatal period. Thirty-nine patients (78%) presented with hypoketotic hypoglycemia, whereas 11 (22%) presented with chronic problems consisting of failure to thrive, feeding difficulties, cholestatic liver disease, and/or hypotonia.

den Boer et al. (2002) found that, in retrospect, 82% of the patients who presented with an acute metabolic derangement had also had a combination of chronic nonspecific symptoms before the metabolic crises, and concluded that LCHAD deficiency often presents with chronic nonspecific symptoms, making early diagnosis difficult in the absence of the classical metabolic derangement.

den Boer et al. (2002) reported high mortality (38%) in their series of 50 LCHAD-deficient patients, all deaths occurring before or within 3 months after diagnosis. Morbidity among survivors was also high, with recurrent metabolic crises and muscle problems despite therapy.
den Boer et al. (2002) concluded that survival in LCHAD deficiency can be improved by prompt diagnosis but that morbidity remains alarmingly high despite current therapeutic regimens.
den Boer et al. (2002) described LCHAD deficiency as a rare autosomal recessive inborn error of fatty acid oxidation.

To study how pigmentary retinopathy arises in LCHAD deficiency, Tyni et al. (2002) cultured porcine retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells. These cells shortened [U-13C]-hexadecanoic acid normally and produced acetylcarnitine. They also had LCHAD enzyme activity, expressed the mitochondrial trifunctional protein (MTP) and could take up carnitine. In human retinal sections, MTP antibodies labeled the RPE, photoreceptors and ganglion cells. The authors concluded that this was strong in vitro evidence for mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation in the RPE. They noted that further studies were needed to clarify whether the pathway also acts in the retina in vivo.

Jones et al. (2003) used an in vitro model to study the effects of dietary treatment in LCHAD deficiency. They grew cultured skin fibroblasts from LCHAD-deficient and normal individuals in media supplemented with physiologic combinations of the medium-chain fatty acids octanoate and decanoate and the long-chain fatty acid palmitate, and measured 3-hydroxy-fatty acids in the medium by stable-isotope dilution gas chromatography/mass spectrometry. Addition of medium-chain fatty acids decreased the accumulation of long-chain fatty acid oxidation intermediates in LCHAD-deficient cells, both in untreated medium and with added palmitate, and decanoate alone was more effective than octanoate alone.

Jones et al. (2003) found that a 1:3 ratio of octanoate to decanoate worked best over an extended time in LCHAD-deficient fibroblasts in untreated medium, whereas a 1:1 ratio worked best in medium containing palmitate. Because all dietary medium-chain triglyceride preparations contain more octanoate than decanoate, the authors suggested that a preparation higher in decanoate may be more effective in reducing the accumulation of potentially toxic long-chain 3-hydroxy-fatty acids in LCHAD deficiency.
Baskin et al. (2010) reported a 22-month-old child with LCHAD deficiency who was identified on expanded newborn screening by an abnormal acylcarnitine pattern with increased C14OH.

Baskin et al. (2010) found that a child with LCHAD deficiency was homozygous for the common HADHA mutation c.1526G>C (p.Glu510Gln). The father was heterozygous for the mutation, but the mother did not carry it. Short tandem repeat testing with markers covering both the short and long arms of chromosome 2 showed that the child had paternal uniparental isodisomy of chromosome 2.

Baskin et al. (2010) showed by short tandem repeat analysis that homozygosity for an HADHA mutation in a child with LCHAD deficiency resulted from paternal uniparental isodisomy of chromosome 2. They emphasized the importance of parental testing when a patient with an autosomal recessive disorder is homozygous, because of its impact on genetic counseling.

Elizondo et al. (2020) measured plasma acylcarnitines in 11 treated patients with LCHAD/TFP deficiency who were on a controlled low long-chain-fat diet with MCT. After a 10-hour overnight fast, C18:1-OH was the most prominent long-chain acylcarnitine (0.56 +/- 0.52 umol/L; reference 0.00-0.05). C16-OH and C18-OH were also above the reference range. C18:1-OH fell by 59% after breakfast and rose by only 20% after 45 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise, a response that was fairly consistent across subjects.

Elizondo et al. (2020) found that the newborn-screening discriminating ratios for LCHAD deficiency, C16-OH/C16 and C18-OH/C18, stayed elevated in treated patients. They concluded that disease-specific acylcarnitines vary widely through the day with feeding, fasting and activity. They therefore recommended that blood for plasma acylcarnitine analysis be collected under standardized conditions, timed in relation to food intake and physical activity.

Elizondo et al. (2020) reported that 9 of 11 patients with LCHAD/TFP deficiency were either homozygous or compound heterozygous for the common HADHA variant c.1528G>C (E510Q). Two patients did not carry it. One was a female with c.901G>A (G301S) and an unidentified second allele. The other was a male compound heterozygous for c.1150-1G>T and c.208T>C (S70P). These variants had previously been reported as pathogenic and associated with a TFP deficiency phenotype.

Elizondo et al. (2020) found that the 9 patients carrying the common c.1528G>C variant on at least one HADHA allele had consistently higher C16-OH, C18-OH and C18:1-OH levels than the 2 patients without it, who had a TFP deficiency phenotype. Mean fasting C18:0-OH was 0.229 umol/L in carriers versus 0.016 umol/L in non-carriers, but the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.09). The authors suggested that variants which destabilize the protein and abolish mitochondrial TFP expression produce low hydroxyacylcarnitine levels because hydratase activity is absent, so the acylcarnitine profile more closely resembles that of VLCAD deficiency.

Elizondo et al. (2020) found that across 30 treated patients with long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorders, including LCHAD deficiency, feeding consistently suppressed disease-specific acylcarnitines by about 60%. Fasting plasma free fatty acids correlated with the fasting sum of long-chain acylcarnitines. The authors concluded that this supports fasting avoidance and frequent meals. All patients tolerated moderate exercise, which the authors said supported current recommendations for patients to be physically active.

Guffon et al. (2021) retrospectively studied 18 French patients (8 female, 10 male) with long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorders (VLCAD, LCHAD, CACT, CPTII, and MTP deficiencies). The patients received triheptanoin through early access for a median of 22 months (range, 9-228 months), and at last consultation it supplied 15 to 35% of daily calories. In the year after starting triheptanoin, patients reported less intermittent snacking and fewer nocturnal meals. Three patients no longer had severe hypoglycemic events. Ten of 12 pediatric and 4 of 6 adult patients reported less fatigue and fewer, less severe episodes of myalgia. Five of the 6 patients who had needed a wheelchair no longer needed it. Emergency hospitalizations decreased, with none in pediatric patients, and annual days of emergency home care fell from 286 to 51. Adverse events were limited to digestive problems that resolved over time. The authors suggested that long-term triheptanoin is safe and markedly improves symptoms and quality of life.
